about.title: About

content.heading: We write down the small good things
content.text: A weekly notebook of recipes we cook, a garden that mostly works, things made by hand and evenings off.

content.heading: How Daybook started
content.text: Daybook started as a notebook shared by two friends: what we cooked, what came up in the garden, what we made with our hands and how we spent the evenings. It still works the same way, just with more readers. A new story goes up every Sunday morning.

items.title: We make it before we write it
items.text: Every recipe is cooked at least three times in a home kitchen, and every project is finished, before its story goes up.

items.title: Nobody pays to be here
items.text: No sponsored stories and no affiliate links. If we recommend something, we bought it ourselves.

items.title: Small, on purpose
items.text: One to three stories a week, out on Sunday mornings, so there is time to test each one properly.

content: Start with a section, follow a series from its first part, or open the latest stories on the homepage. If something we wrote did not work for you, tell us: most of our best stories began as a reader's question.

contact.title: Contact
content: We read everything and answer most of it, usually within three working days. Pick the address that fits and it will reach the right person.
Questions about a recipe, a project that went sideways, or just to say it worked.
Two or three sentences on what you made, and one photo of it. We reply to every pitch, yes or no.
Spotted a wrong weight or a missing step? Tell us which story and we will correct it within a week.
Can I share one of your recipes?
Yes, with a link back to the story. Please don't copy the whole method; a photo of your own version and a sentence about it is perfect.
No. Nothing on Daybook is paid for, and we don't use affiliate links.
Please do. The bread series started as a reader's question.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
content: This is a sample privacy policy for the Daybook demo. Replace it with your own before you publish your site.
When you leave a comment, we keep your name, your email address and what you wrote. When you write to us, we keep your message so we can answer it.
Only to run this site and to reply to you. We never sell it or share it with anyone for their own use.
Ask us at any time for a copy of what we hold about you, or to delete it.

twenty-minute-tomato-penne.title: Twenty-minute tomato penne
twenty-minute-tomato-penne.excerpt: Tinned tomatoes, a lot of garlic and the pasta water you were about to pour away.
content: This is the dinner we make when the fridge is nearly empty and nobody wants to think. It takes as long as the pasta takes, and it tastes like it took longer.
For two hungry people or three polite ones:
One 400 g tin of chopped tomatoes
Six cloves of garlic, thinly sliced
Salt, and a little sugar if the tomatoes are sharp
The sauce, while the water boils

Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over a low heat and add the garlic. Let it turn pale gold slowly; if it browns, it turns bitter. Add the chilli, then the tomatoes and a good pinch of salt, and let it bubble gently while the pasta cooks.

Scoop out a mug of the pasta water before you drain. Tip the penne into the sauce with a splash of that water and stir over the heat for a minute. The starch makes the sauce cling, so it coats the pasta instead of pooling underneath it.
Save the pasta water. It is the difference between pasta with sauce and a sauce that holds the pasta.
Tear in the basil off the heat, taste, and serve straight from the pan.

a-week-of-dinners-from-one-veg-box.title: A week of dinners from one veg box
a-week-of-dinners-from-one-veg-box.excerpt: One delivery, seven dinners, and a plan for the vegetable nobody asked for.
content: A veg box is a lovely idea until Thursday, when half of it is still in the crisper drawer. This is the plan we use to get through a whole box before the next one arrives, with the most delicate things first.
Sort it the day it arrives
Unpack everything onto the counter and make three piles: what wilts in two days, what keeps for a week, and what keeps for a month. Herbs and salad leaves go first; roots and squash wait their turn.
Monday: a big salad with the most fragile leaves and herbs.
Tuesday: the tomatoes go into a quick sauce, before they soften.
Wednesday: greens wilted into pasta or eggs.
Thursday: a tray of roasted roots, half of it saved for Friday.
Friday: the leftover roots in a soup with a tin of beans.
Saturday: something slow with the squash.
Every box has one: the kohlrabi, the celeriac, the third cabbage in a row. Roast it, grate it into a slaw, or turn it into soup. If all else fails, it goes into Friday's soup and nobody notices.
Keep a list on the fridge
Write what is left on a sticky note on the fridge door and cross things off as you go. It takes ten seconds a day, and it is the single thing that stopped us throwing vegetables away.

twelve-pencils-is-enough.title: Twelve pencils is enough: a starter kit for sketching
twelve-pencils-is-enough.excerpt: Skip the 72-colour tin. The small set we would buy again, and why each one earns its place.
content: The big tins look generous and end up as a box of colours you never use. Twelve pencils, chosen on purpose, will take you further, and you will learn far more about mixing.
Two yellows: one warm, one cool
Two reds: a scarlet and a crimson
Two blues: an ultramarine and a sky blue
Two greens: a deep one and a sap green
A burnt sienna and a raw umber for anything earthy
A cool grey, and a black you will barely use

Coloured pencils are translucent, so colours mix on the paper. A light layer of yellow under blue gives a green you could not buy. Press lightly, build slowly, and save the hard pressure for the last layer.
A smooth, heavy paper takes many more layers than printer paper. One good sketchbook will do more for your drawings than any extra pencil.

leaf-mould-free-compost.title: Leaf mould: free compost from autumn's mess
leaf-mould-free-compost.excerpt: Bag the leaves, poke a few holes, and forget about them until next autumn.
content: Every autumn the leaves fall, and every autumn people bag them up and throw them away. Keep them instead: in a year they turn into a dark, crumbly mulch that gardeners pay good money for.
Rake the leaves after rain, or water them as you go. They need to be damp to break down. Leave out evergreen leaves and anything thick and waxy, which takes years.
Pack them into an old compost bag, tie the top loosely, and poke a dozen holes in the sides with a fork. Stand the bags somewhere out of the way and forget them.
After a year you have a mulch to spread around plants and on bare soil. Leave it a second year and it becomes fine enough to mix into seed compost.

an-evening-without-screens.title: An evening without screens, one candle at a time
an-evening-without-screens.excerpt: The phone goes in a drawer at eight. What we did with the hours that came back.
content: For one month, our phones went into a kitchen drawer at eight o'clock and stayed there until morning. We expected to be bored. Mostly, we were surprised by how long an evening is.
Phones in the drawer at eight, alarms set first.
The television stays off on weeknights.
One lamp and one candle instead of the big light.
Anything we wanted to look up went on a paper list for the morning.

Long dinners. Books finished for the first time in years. A jigsaw that took a fortnight. Letters to people we had only been messaging. And, more than once, an early night that did not feel like giving up.
We let ourselves off on weekends now, but the drawer is still the phone's home after dinner on weeknights. The candle stayed too.

lavender-balm-in-an-afternoon.title: Make a lavender balm in an afternoon
lavender-balm-in-an-afternoon.excerpt: Beeswax, oil and dried lavender. The only hard part is waiting for it to set.
content: A small tin of balm for dry hands and elbows takes one afternoon, four ingredients and no special equipment. Make a batch and you have presents for a season.
100 ml of a light oil, such as sunflower or almond
Small tins or jars with lids
Warm the oil and lavender in a bowl over a pan of barely simmering water for an hour. Keep it gentle: the oil should never smoke. Strain it through a fine sieve or a clean cloth.

Return the oil to the bowl, add the beeswax and stir until it melts. Pour into the tins straight away and leave them uncovered until they set, about an hour. More beeswax makes a firmer balm; less makes it softer.

overnight-oats-five-ways.title: Overnight oats, five ways
overnight-oats-five-ways.excerpt: One base, made on Sunday night, eaten all week without getting bored of it.
content: Weekday mornings are short. Five jars made on Sunday night mean breakfast is the one decision you don't have to make.
For each jar: 50 g of rolled oats, 100 ml of milk, two tablespoons of yogurt and a pinch of salt. Stir, close the lid and leave it in the fridge overnight. It keeps for four days.
Fig and raspberry, with a drizzle of honey.
Grated apple and cinnamon, stirred in the night before.
Banana and a spoon of peanut butter.
Frozen berries, which thaw into the oats overnight.
Orange zest, toasted almonds and a few dates.
Oats keep soaking up milk in the fridge. Loosen a jar with a splash more milk in the morning and stir it well.

the-other-half-of-the-onion.title: The other half of the onion
the-other-half-of-the-onion.excerpt: A note stuck to our fridge since the first week of Daybook.
content: Most of cooking is deciding what to do with the other half of the onion.
It has been on our fridge since the first week of Daybook. It is still true. Wrap the other half tightly and use it within two days, in tomorrow's eggs, a quick pickle or the base of a soup.

radishes-in-thirty-days.title: Radishes in thirty days, even on a balcony
radishes-in-thirty-days.excerpt: The fastest crop we know, a pot deep enough for it, and when to pull them before they turn woody.
content: If you have never grown anything to eat, start with radishes. They come up in days, they are ready in about a month, and they forgive almost everything.
A pot and a sunny spot
Any pot at least 15 cm deep will do, with holes in the bottom. Fill it with multipurpose compost and put it where it gets sun for half the day.
Sow seeds a finger's width apart and a centimetre deep, and water them in. Sow a short row every two weeks rather than the whole packet at once, so they don't all arrive together.
Radishes are best the size of a marble to a cherry. Left too long, they split and turn woody and hot. Check them from the third week and pull the biggest first.

what-to-sow-in-october.title: What to sow in October (yes, really)
what-to-sow-in-october.excerpt: Garlic, broad beans and a tray of winter salad leaves for the windowsill.
content: The garden looks finished in October, but a few crops want to go in now. They sit quietly through winter and get a head start in spring.

Split a bulb into cloves and push them into the soil, pointed end up, about 15 cm apart and just below the surface. Garlic needs a cold spell to form proper bulbs, which is exactly what winter gives it.
Hardy varieties sown now crop earlier than spring sowings and are often ahead of the blackfly. Sow them 5 cm deep and 20 cm apart.
A tray of mixed leaves on a bright windowsill gives you something green to pick through the darkest weeks. Cut them young and they will grow back two or three times.

sketch-the-room-before-you-move-a-thing.title: Sketch the room before you move a thing
sketch-the-room-before-you-move-a-thing.excerpt: A tape measure, squared paper and twenty minutes save a whole weekend of shifting furniture.
content: Before you drag the sofa across the room for the third time, draw the room. Twenty minutes with a pencil tells you what will fit, and what will only fit if nobody wants to open the door.
Measure the walls, then the gaps
Measure each wall, then the doors, windows and radiators along it. Note which way each door swings: a door's sweep is the space people forget.
On squared paper, one square to 10 cm works for most rooms. Draw the outline, mark the doors and windows, and shade the door sweeps so you keep them clear.
Draw each piece of furniture to the same scale on another sheet and cut it out. Now you can move the paper sofa around in seconds, and lift the real one only once.

one-desk-two-hobbies.title: One desk, two hobbies
one-desk-two-hobbies.excerpt: A drawer for drawing, a drawer for sewing, and one rule about what lives on top.
content: Our spare room is also an office, a sewing room and a drawing studio. It works because of a few small rules, not because it is big.
Everything for one hobby lives in one drawer or one box, so starting means opening it and finishing means closing it. If a hobby outgrows its drawer, something in it has to go.
Only what you are using today sits on the desk. At the end of the day it goes back in its drawer, even if you will take it out again tomorrow.

plant-tulips-now-for-april.title: Plant tulips now for April
plant-tulips-now-for-april.excerpt: Bulbs in the ground by November, three times as deep as they are tall, and colour when you need it most.
content: Tulips go in later than other spring bulbs, which makes them the perfect job for a cold, clear afternoon in October or November.
Plant each bulb pointed end up, about three times as deep as the bulb is tall. Deep planting keeps them steady in spring winds and helps them come back the following year.
Layer them in a deep pot with the bulbs almost touching. Keep the compost just moist through winter and put the pot somewhere you will see it every morning in April.

sweet-dough-for-sunday-buns.title: Sweet dough for Sunday buns
sweet-dough-for-sunday-buns.excerpt: The same starter, some butter and cinnamon, and a tray of buns that rise overnight while you sleep.
content: The last part of the series is a reward. The starter that made your baguettes makes a soft, sweet dough just as happily. Shape it on Saturday evening and bake it for Sunday breakfast.

Mix everything except the butter, knead for five minutes, then work the butter in a little at a time. It will look hopeless, then suddenly come together. Leave it covered for four to six hours, until puffy.

Roll the dough into a large rectangle, spread it with 60 g of soft butter mixed with 80 g of brown sugar and two teaspoons of cinnamon, and roll it up from the long side. Cut it into twelve and set them in a lined tin.
Rise overnight, bake in the morning
Cover the tin and leave it in the fridge overnight. In the morning, let it warm up for an hour, then bake at 190 °C for 20 to 25 minutes, until golden.

packing-light-for-two-days-away.title: Packing light for two days away
packing-light-for-two-days-away.excerpt: One bag, one hat, and nothing you will carry home unused.
content: A weekend away should start the moment you shut the front door, not after an hour of packing. This is the list we use, and it fits in one small bag.
One change of clothes, plus what you travel in
A jumper that goes with everything
Shoes you can walk in all day
Chargers and a toothbrush in a single pouch
If you didn't use something on your last two trips, it doesn't come on this one. Two weekends of that and your bag gets lighter on its own.

a-salad-worth-the-chopping.title: A salad worth the chopping
a-salad-worth-the-chopping.excerpt: Cherry tomatoes, sweetcorn and black beans, dressed while the corn is still warm.
content: This is a salad that eats like a meal. It keeps for a day in the fridge, so it is just as good for tomorrow's lunch.
Two corn cobs, or a small tin of sweetcorn
One tin of black beans, rinsed
A punnet of cherry tomatoes, halved
A bunch of coriander or parsley
The juice of two limes and three tablespoons of olive oil
Char the corn in a dry pan until it blisters in places, then slice it off the cob. Toss it with everything else while it's still warm: the beans and onion soak up the dressing far better that way.

shaping-a-weekend-baguette.title: Shaping a weekend baguette
shaping-a-weekend-baguette.excerpt: Three loaves shaped by hand, with a crust that crackles as it cools. The part that matters takes four minutes a loaf.
content: Part one left you with a starter that bubbles on schedule. This week it earns its keep. Start the dough on Saturday morning, let it rise slowly in the fridge overnight, and bake on Sunday before lunch.
The cold night does two jobs: it gives the bread more flavour, and it firms the dough up, so it is far easier to shape. The schedule helps you twice.
For three baguettes, about 320 g of dough each:
100 g active starter, fed 6 to 8 hours before
A bench scraper, a floured tea towel and a baking tray

Tip the dough onto an unfloured counter and cut it into three pieces. Fold each one into a loose log and leave it seam side up under a tea towel. Twenty minutes is enough for the dough to relax; skip the rest and it will fight you, springing back every time you roll it.
Tension is the whole trick. A baguette that holds its shape in the oven was shaped tightly on the counter.
Flatten a piece into a rectangle, with a long side towards you.
Fold the top third down and press the edge in with your fingertips.
Fold the top edge down to the bottom and seal it with the heel of your hand.
Roll from the middle out with both hands until the loaf is about 35 cm long.
Keep a little flour on the counter, not on the dough. You want some grip: on a floured surface the loaf skids instead of stretching.

Heat the oven to 250 °C with the tray inside for 45 minutes. Score each loaf with three long, shallow cuts, pour a cup of boiling water into a tin on the bottom shelf, and bake for 12 minutes. Take the water out, turn the oven down to 230 °C and bake for 12 to 15 minutes more, until the crust is deep brown and the bottom sounds hollow.
Leave them to cool for at least 20 minutes. They will crackle while they do. That sound is the reward.

dried-flowers-that-last-all-winter.title: Dried flowers that last all winter
dried-flowers-that-last-all-winter.excerpt: Hang them upside down somewhere dark and dry, and the summer garden keeps you company until spring.
content: The last flowers of the season don't have to go on the compost. Dried, they keep their shape and much of their colour for months.
Cut flowers just before they are fully open, on a dry day, after the morning dew has gone. Lavender, statice, strawflowers, hydrangeas and grasses all dry well.

Strip the lower leaves, tie the stems in small bunches and hang them upside down somewhere dark, dry and airy, such as a cupboard or under the stairs. Two to three weeks later they are papery and ready.

hand-dipped-beeswax-candles.title: Hand-dipped beeswax candles
hand-dipped-beeswax-candles.excerpt: A tall pot, a length of wick and about thirty dips. A quiet way to spend a winter afternoon.
content: Dipped candles grow one thin layer at a time, which makes them slow in the best way. An afternoon gives you a dozen pairs, and they burn longer and cleaner than most candles you can buy.
Beeswax pellets, about 1 kg for a dozen pairs
Cotton wick, sized for 2 cm candles
A tall tin or jug that stands in a pan of water
Small weights, such as washers, for the wick ends
Something to hang them from while they cool
Melt the wax in the tall tin, standing in a pan of simmering water, never over a direct flame. It is ready when it is clear and liquid, around 70 °C.

Tie a weight to each end of a length of wick and fold it over a stick, so you dip two candles at once. Dip, lift, let them cool for a minute, and dip again. After about thirty dips they are thick enough. Trim the bases flat while they are still warm.

a-starter-you-wont-neglect.title: A starter you won't neglect
a-starter-you-wont-neglect.excerpt: Flour, water and a jar in the fridge. Feed it once a week and it will raise your bread for years.
content: This is the first part of Bread, step by step. Before any loaf, you need a starter: a jar of flour and water that wild yeast has moved into. It sounds fussy. It is mostly waiting.

Stir 50 g of wholemeal flour with 50 g of water in a clean jar and leave it, loosely covered, somewhere warm. Every day for a week, throw away half and feed what is left with another 50 g of flour and 50 g of water.
Around day five or six it starts to rise and fall on a schedule, doubling within a few hours of each feed and smelling pleasantly sour. That rhythm is what you are waiting for.

Once it is lively, the fridge slows it right down. Feed it once a week, and take it out the night before you bake so it wakes up. A forgotten starter is rarely dead: two or three feeds usually bring it back.

the-25-minute-hour.title: The 25-minute hour
the-25-minute-hour.excerpt: How a kitchen timer fixed our desk days: work for twenty-five minutes, stop for five, and actually stop.
content: Working from home made our days longer and less useful. What helped wasn't an app. It was a kitchen timer and one rule about the breaks.

Set the timer for twenty-five minutes and work on one thing only. When it rings, stop, even mid-sentence, and take five minutes away from the desk. After four rounds, take a proper break of half an hour.
Make the break a real one
The rule that made it work: no screens in the five minutes. Fill the kettle, stretch, water a plant, look out of the window. Coming back to the desk feels like starting fresh rather than carrying on.

a-bag-of-peppers-three-dinners.title: A bag of peppers, three dinners
a-bag-of-peppers-three-dinners.excerpt: Roast them all on Sunday, then turn them into eggs, pasta and a soup through the week.
content: When peppers are cheap at the market, buy a bag and roast the lot on Sunday. They keep for five days in a jar under oil, and they make three very different dinners.
Slice six peppers into wide strips, toss them with olive oil, salt and a spoonful of tomato paste, and roast at 200 °C for 35 minutes, until the edges catch.
Eggs baked in a pan of peppers and tinned tomatoes, with bread to mop it up.
Blended with garlic and olive oil into a sauce for pasta.
Simmered with stock and a potato into a smooth, bright soup.

saving-seed-from-your-best-tomatoes.title: Saving seed from your best tomatoes
saving-seed-from-your-best-tomatoes.excerpt: Next year's plants are already in this year's best fruit. A jar, some water and a few days are all it takes.
content: If one tomato plant did better than the rest this year, keep its seeds. Old varieties come back true from seed, so next year's plants will be just like it.

Squeeze the seeds and jelly of a ripe fruit into a jar with a little water and leave it for three or four days. A layer of mould on top is normal: the ferment removes the gel that stops the seeds from sprouting.
Rinse the seeds in a sieve, spread them on a plate and let them dry for a week. Store them in a labelled paper envelope somewhere cool and dry. They keep for several years.
